Lecture 30

First-order PDEs and characteristics

Lecture objectives

We solve linear first-order equations along characteristic curves and prove existence and uniqueness for transport with decay and a source, at a constant and at a variable speed. We prove that data on a noncharacteristic curve determine a solution near each of its points.

Lecture 29 derived partial differential equations from balance laws. In this lecture we solve the linear equations of first order. Such an equation prescribes the rate of change of the unknown along one direction at each point. Along the curves that follow this direction, the characteristic curves, it becomes an ordinary differential equation of Lectures 4 and 5.

30.1 Transport at a constant speed

All equations of this lecture before Section 30.4 have the evolution form ut+a(x,t) ux+γ(x,t) u=f(x,t),u_t+a(x,t)\,u_x+\gamma(x,t)\,u=f(x,t),ut​+a(x,t)ux​+γ(x,t)u=f(x,t),(30.1) with an advection speed a,aa, a decay rate γ\gammaγ (negative values mean growth) and a source f,ff, all real functions.

Definition 30.1 (Cauchy problem and classical solution). Let a,aa, γ\gammaγ and fff be continuous on R×[0,∞),\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞), and let u0∈C1(R).u_0\in C^1(\R)u0​∈C1(R). A classical solution of the Cauchy problem for (30.1) with the initial data u0u_0u0​ is a function uuu that is continuous on R×[0,∞),\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞), has continuous first partial derivatives on R×(0,∞),\R\times(0,\infty)R×(0,∞), satisfies (30.1) at every point of R×(0,∞),\R\times(0,\infty)R×(0,∞), and satisfies u(x,0)=u0(x)for every x∈R.u(x,0)=u_0(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\R .u(x,0)=u0​(x)for every x∈R.(30.2)

The equation is required only for t>0,t>0t>0, and the data are reached by continuity. This is Lecture 29’s notion of a classical solution, for an equation of first order.

The simplest equation of this form describes a substance carried along a river by a flow with the constant velocity a.aa. Let u(x,t)u(x,t)u(x,t) be its concentration, the amount per unit length. The amount that passes the position xxx per unit time is the flux j=au,j=auj=au, and, as in Lecture 29, the amount in [x1,x2][x_1,x_2][x1​,x2​] changes only by the fluxes through its ends:  ⁣d ⁣dt∫x1x2u(x,t) ⁣dx=j(x1,t)−j(x2,t)=−∫x1x2∂x(au(x,t)) ⁣dx.\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\int_{x_1}^{x_2}u(x,t)\dd x=j(x_1,t)-j(x_2,t) =-\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\partial_x\bigl(au(x,t)\bigr)\dd x .dtd​∫x1​x2​​u(x,t)dx=j(x1​,t)−j(x2​,t)=−∫x1​x2​​∂x​(au(x,t))dx. Let uuu have continuous first partial derivatives. As in Lecture 29, utu_tut​ is bounded on closed boxes, rule I2 of Lecture 22 moves the time derivative inside the integral, and the localization lemma gives ut+(au)x=0.u_t+(au)_x=0ut​+(au)x​=0. With a constant speed this is the transport equation ut+aux=0.u_t+au_x=0 .ut​+aux​=0.(30.3)

The left side of (30.3) is a rate of change along a line. Fix a number ξ\xiξ and follow the point x=ξ+at,x=\xi+atx=ξ+at, which moves with the flow. By the chain rule (GM 36),  ⁣d ⁣dt u(ξ+at,t)=ux(ξ+at,t) a+ut(ξ+at,t).\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\,u(\xi+at,t)=u_x(\xi+at,t)\,a+u_t(\xi+at,t).dtd​u(ξ+at,t)=ux​(ξ+at,t)a+ut​(ξ+at,t).(30.4) So (30.3) says that uuu is constant along each line x−at=ξx-at=\xix−at=ξ of the (x,t)(x,t)(x,t) plane. These lines are the characteristics of (30.3). The number ξ\xiξ is the foot of the characteristic, the point where it meets the initial line t=0.t=0t=0.

Proposition 30.2 (Transport at a constant speed). Let a∈Ra\in\Ra∈R and u0∈C1(R).u_0\in C^1(\R)u0​∈C1(R). The Cauchy problem for (30.3) with the data u0u_0u0​ has exactly one classical solution, u(x,t)=u0(x−at).u(x,t)=u_0(x-at).u(x,t)=u0​(x−at).(30.5)

Proof. First, the formula is a solution. It is continuous with continuous first partial derivatives on R2,\R^2R2, and the chain rule gives ut=−a u0′(x−at),ux=u0′(x−at),u_t=-a\,u_0'(x-at),\qquad u_x=u_0'(x-at),ut​=−au0′​(x−at),ux​=u0′​(x−at), so ut+aux=0.u_t+au_x=0ut​+aux​=0. At t=0t=0t=0 it equals u0(x).u_0(x)u0​(x).

Next, uniqueness. Let uuu be a classical solution, and fix ξ∈R.\xi\in\Rξ∈R. The function U(t)=u(ξ+at,t)U(t)=u(\xi+at,t)U(t)=u(ξ+at,t) is continuous on [0,∞).[0,\infty)[0,∞). By (30.4) and (30.3) it is differentiable on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) with U′(t)=0.U'(t)=0U′(t)=0. For every t>0t>0t>0 the mean value theorem (GM 9) on [0,t][0,t][0,t] gives U(t)=U(0)=u0(ξ).U(t)=U(0)=u_0(\xi)U(t)=U(0)=u0​(ξ). A given point (x,t)(x,t)(x,t) with t≥0t\ge0t≥0 lies on the characteristic with the foot ξ=x−at,\xi=x-atξ=x−at, so u(x,t)=u0(x−at).u(x,t)=u_0(x-at)u(x,t)=u0​(x−at). ■

30.2 Transport with decay and a source

Many substances are carried by a flow and decay at the same time: a radioactive isotope, a reacting chemical, or bacteria in a river. Suppose that the substance decays at the constant rate γ≥0,\gamma\ge0γ≥0, so that the amount γu ⁣dx\gamma u\dd xγudx is lost per unit time in a short interval of length  ⁣dx,\dd xdx, and that it is added at the rate f(x,t)f(x,t)f(x,t) per unit length and unit time. The balance on [x1,x2][x_1,x_2][x1​,x2​] gains the term ∫x1x2(f−γu) ⁣dx\int_{x_1}^{x_2}(f-\gamma u)\dd x∫x1​x2​​(f−γu)dx on the right, and the localization gives ut+aux+γu=f(x,t),u_t+au_x+\gamma u=f(x,t),ut​+aux​+γu=f(x,t),(30.6) the evolution form (30.1) with constant aaa and γ.\gammaγ.

Along the characteristic with the foot ξ\xiξ we put U(t)=u(ξ+at,t).U(t)=u(\xi+at,t)U(t)=u(ξ+at,t). By (30.4), equation (30.6) becomes the linear equation U′(t)+γU(t)=f(ξ+at,t),U(0)=u0(ξ).U'(t)+\gamma U(t)=f(\xi+at,t),\qquad U(0)=u_0(\xi).U′(t)+γU(t)=f(ξ+at,t),U(0)=u0​(ξ). Lecture 5 solves it by variation of constants: U(t)=e−γtu0(ξ)+∫0te−γ(t−τ)f(ξ+aτ,τ) ⁣dτ.U(t)=\ee^{-\gamma t}u_0(\xi)+\int_0^t\ee^{-\gamma(t-\tau)}f(\xi+a\tau,\tau)\dd\tau .U(t)=e−γtu0​(ξ)+∫0t​e−γ(t−τ)f(ξ+aτ,τ)dτ. The variable τ\tauτ is the source time. With ξ=x−at\xi=x-atξ=x−at the point ξ+aτ\xi+a\tauξ+aτ becomes x−a(t−τ),x-a(t-\tau)x−a(t−τ), the place where the substance that arrives at xxx at the time ttt was at the time τ.\tauτ. This suggests the formula of the theorem below. To prove that it is a classical solution we differentiate an integral whose upper limit and integrand both depend on the variables.

Example 30.5 (A pollutant pulse in a river). We follow a pulse of a decaying substance down a river. Its amount is umσ2π e−γt,u_{\mathrm m}\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\,\ee^{-\gamma t}um​σ2π​e−γt, by the Gaussian integral of GM 38.

A pulse of the width σ=100 m\sigma=100\,\mathrm mσ=100m passes the station in a time of order σ/a=200 s,\sigma/a=200\,\mathrm sσ/a=200s, during which the decay changes it little. 30.3 Variable speed

When the speed of the flow changes with the position or the time, the characteristics are no longer straight lines. Their slopes are prescribed instead by an ordinary differential equation.

Definition 30.7 (Characteristic curves). Let aaa have continuous first partial derivatives on R2.\R^2R2. 30.4 Data on a curve

So far the data were given on the line t=0.t=0t=0. We now give them on a curve in a plane with the coordinates (x,y),(x,y)(x,y), and ask when they determine a solution. The evolution form (30.1) is the case y=ty=ty=t and b=1.b=1b=1. The characteristic curves of (30.18) are the solutions of the autonomous system  ⁣dx ⁣dμ=a(x,y), ⁣dy ⁣dμ=b(x,y),\frac{\dd x}{\dd\mu}=a(x,y),\qquad\frac{\dd y}{\dd\mu}=b(x,y),dμdx​=a(x,y),dμdy​=b(x,y),(30.19) with a parameter μ\muμ that need not be a time. Along such a curve  ⁣du(x(μ),y(μ))/ ⁣dμ=aux+buy,\dd u(x(\mu),y(\mu))/\dd\mu=au_x+bu_ydu(x(μ),y(μ))/dμ=aux​+buy​, by the chain rule. So on the curve (30.18) becomes  ⁣du ⁣dμ=f−γu,\frac{\dd u}{\dd\mu}=f-\gamma u ,dμdu​=f−γu, a third equation coupled to (30.19).

The data are given on a curve ξ↦(x0(ξ),y0(ξ))\xi\mapsto(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi))ξ↦(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ)) in U,UU, ξ∈J,\xi\in Jξ∈J, an open interval, with continuous derivatives and with (x0′,y0′)≠(0,0):(x_0',y_0')\ne(0,0)(x0′​,y0′​)=(0,0): u(x0(ξ),y0(ξ))=u0(ξ)(ξ∈J),u\bigl(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi)\bigr)=u_0(\xi)\qquad(\xi\in J),u(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ))=u0​(ξ)(ξ∈J),(30.20) with u0∈C1(J).u_0\in C^1(J)u0​∈C1(J). For the line t=0t=0t=0 we have x0(ξ)=ξx_0(\xi)=\xix0​(ξ)=ξ and y0(ξ)=0,y_0(\xi)=0y0​(ξ)=0, and (30.20) is (30.2).

Suppose that a solution with continuous first derivatives exists near the curve. Differentiating the data along the curve, and evaluating the equation on it, gives two linear equations for the two values uxu_xux​ and uyu_yuy​ at a point of the curve: x0′(ξ) ux+y0′(ξ) uy=u0′(ξ),a ux+b uy=f−γu0(ξ),x_0'(\xi)\,u_x+y_0'(\xi)\,u_y=u_0'(\xi),\qquad a\,u_x+b\,u_y=f-\gamma u_0(\xi),x0′​(ξ)ux​+y0′​(ξ)uy​=u0′​(ξ),aux​+buy​=f−γu0​(ξ), with a,aa, b,bb, γ\gammaγ and fff evaluated at (x0(ξ),y0(ξ)).(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi))(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ)). The determinant of this system decides whether the data and the equation fix the gradient on the curve.

Definition 30.11 (Noncharacteristic data). The data curve is noncharacteristic at ξ\xiξ if Δ(ξ)=x0′(ξ) b(x0(ξ),y0(ξ))−y0′(ξ) a(x0(ξ),y0(ξ))≠0.\Delta(\xi)=x_0'(\xi)\,b\bigl(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi)\bigr)-y_0'(\xi)\,a\bigl(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi)\bigr)\ne0 .Δ(ξ)=x0′​(ξ)b(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ))−y0′​(ξ)a(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ))=0.(30.21)

The number Δ(ξ)\Delta(\xi)Δ(ξ) is the determinant of the matrix with the rows (x0′,y0′)(x_0',y_0')(x0′​,y0′​) and (a,b).(a,b)(a,b). It is nonzero exactly when the tangent (x0′,y0′)(x_0',y_0')(x0′​,y0′​) is not parallel to the characteristic direction (a,b),(a,b)(a,b), that is, when the curve is not tangent to the characteristic through that point. For the line t=0t=0t=0 of an evolution equation, Δ=1⋅1−0⋅a=1,\Delta=1\cdot1-0\cdot a=1Δ=1⋅1−0⋅a=1, so the initial line is noncharacteristic at every point.

The proposition is local: it gives a solution in a neighbourhood of one point of the curve. Theorem 30.9 is a global version for the line t=0,t=0t=0, made possible by the linear bound on the speed. The next example shows what goes wrong when Δ=0.\Delta=0Δ=0.

Example 30.13 (Data on a characteristic). We show that data on a characteristic can rule out every solution, or allow infinitely many. For ut+aux=0u_t+au_x=0ut​+aux​=0 with a constant a,aa, give the data on the characteristic x=at:x=atx=at: u(at,t)=u0(t)(t∈R).u(at,t)=u_0(t)\qquad(t\in\R).u(at,t)=u0​(t)(t∈R). In the coordinates (x,y)=(x,t)(x,y)=(x,t)(x,y)=(x,t) the curve is x0(ξ)=aξx_0(\xi)=a\xix0​(ξ)=aξ and y0(ξ)=ξ,y_0(\xi)=\xiy0​(ξ)=ξ, and (30.21) with b=1b=1b=1 gives Δ=a⋅1−1⋅a=0\Delta=a\cdot1-1\cdot a=0Δ=a⋅1−1⋅a=0 at every point (Figure 30.3). By the argument of Proposition 30.2, every solution on R2\R^2R2 with continuous first partial derivatives is constant on each characteristic, so it is u(x,t)=F(x−at)u(x,t)=F(x-at)u(x,t)=F(x−at) with F(ξ)=u(ξ,0)F(\xi)=u(\xi,0)F(ξ)=u(ξ,0) and F∈C1(R).F\in C^1(\R)F∈C1(R). On the data curve x−at=0,x-at=0x−at=0, hence u=F(0)u=F(0)u=F(0) there. Two cases follow.

  • If u0u_0u0​ is not constant, no solution exists.

  • If u0u_0u0​ is the constant u∗,u_*u∗​, every function F(x−at)F(x-at)F(x−at) with F∈C1(R)F\in C^1(\R)F∈C1(R) and F(0)=u∗F(0)=u_*F(0)=u∗​ is a solution. There are infinitely many, and they differ off the data curve.

Data on a characteristic say nothing about the other characteristics, and they must themselves satisfy the equation along the curve. ◃

30.5 The method and its second-order counterpart

The method of characteristics consists of the following steps.

  • Check that the data curve is noncharacteristic, Δ≠0.\Delta\ne0Δ=0.

  • Solve the characteristic system from the data curve.

  • Solve  ⁣du/ ⁣dμ=f−γu\dd u/\dd\mu=f-\gamma udu/dμ=f−γu along each characteristic, with the data at its foot.

  • Check the equation, the data and the region the characteristics cover.

For an equation of first order, data on a noncharacteristic curve, together with the equation, determine the gradient of uuu on the curve. An equation of second order needs the values of uuu and of its derivative across the curve, the Cauchy data on a curve of Lecture 29, which on the line t=0t=0t=0 are uuu and ut.u_tut​. Its characteristic curves are the curves along which these data and the equation fail to determine the second derivatives of u.uu. Lecture 31 finds them for the wave equation utt=c2uxx,u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}utt​=c2uxx​, with the wave speed ccc of Lecture 29. They are the lines x±ct=const,x\pm ct=\text{const}x±ct=const, two families instead of one, as Lecture 29’s classification of hyperbolic equations suggests.

Summary

A linear first-order equation prescribes the rate of change of uuu along the direction (a,b).(a,b)(a,b). Along the characteristic curves it becomes the linear ODE  ⁣du/ ⁣dμ=f−γu.\dd u/\dd\mu=f-\gamma udu/dμ=f−γu. The Cauchy problem has exactly one classical solution, the initial value at the foot carried along the characteristic, damped, plus the source collected along it: by Duhamel’s formula for a constant speed, and with characteristics from an ODE for a speed with a linear bound. Data on a curve determine a solution near every point where the curve is noncharacteristic. Data on a characteristic can rule out every solution or leave it undetermined.

  • Characteristics: for ut+a(x,t)ux+γu=f,u_t+a(x,t)u_x+\gamma u=fut​+a(x,t)ux​+γu=f, the curves  ⁣dX/ ⁣dt=a(X,t).\dd X/\dd t=a(X,t)dX/dt=a(X,t). Along them  ⁣du/ ⁣dt=f−γu.\dd u/\dd t=f-\gamma udu/dt=f−γu. The foot of the characteristic through (x,t)(x,t)(x,t) is Y(0;x,t).Y(0;x,t)Y(0;x,t).

  • Duhamel’s formula: for constant aaa and γ,\gammaγ, u0∈C1(R),u_0\in C^1(\R)u0​∈C1(R), fff and fxf_xfx​ continuous, u=e−γtu0(x−at)+∫0te−γ(t−τ)f(x−a(t−τ),τ) ⁣dτu=\ee^{-\gamma t}u_0(x-at)+\int_0^t\ee^{-\gamma(t-\tau)}f(x-a(t-\tau),\tau)\dd\tauu=e−γtu0​(x−at)+∫0t​e−γ(t−τ)f(x−a(t−τ),τ)dτ is the unique classical solution.

  • Variable speed: for a,aa, γ,\gammaγ, fff with continuous first derivatives, ∣a∣≤A0+A1∣x∣\abs a\le A_0+A_1\abs x∣a∣≤A0​+A1​∣x∣ and u0∈C1(R),u_0\in C^1(\R)u0​∈C1(R), the Cauchy problem has exactly one classical solution: the initial value at the foot Y(0;x,t),Y(0;x,t)Y(0;x,t), damped by e−P(0;x,t),\ee^{-P(0;x,t)}e−P(0;x,t), plus ∫0te−P(τ;x,t)f(Y(τ;x,t),τ) ⁣dτ.\int_0^t\ee^{-P(\tau;x,t)}f(Y(\tau;x,t),\tau)\dd\tau∫0t​e−P(τ;x,t)f(Y(τ;x,t),τ)dτ.

  • Conservation form: ut+(au)x=0,u_t+(au)_x=0ut​+(au)x​=0, that is, γ=ax,\gamma=a_xγ=ax​, describes an amount, as in Example 30.10. The form ut+aux=0u_t+au_x=0ut​+aux​=0 keeps the value carried by each particle.

  • Noncharacteristic data: for coefficients, curve and data with continuous first derivatives, Δ=x0′b−y0′a≠0\Delta=x_0'b-y_0'a\ne0Δ=x0′​b−y0′​a=0 at a point of the data curve gives exactly one solution near that point. Data on a characteristic determine nothing off it and must be compatible along it.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. Solve ut+2ux=0u_t+2u_x=0ut​+2ux​=0 on the line with u(x,0)=x2u(x,0)=x^2u(x,0)=x2. All variables are dimensionless. Which formula satisfies both the equation and the data?

Hint. Follow the characteristic through (x,t)(x,t)(x,t) back to the initial line and read the initial value there.

The curve has speed 222 and reaches the initial line at x−2tx-2tx−2t. The solution is constant along the curve, so u=(x−2t)2u=(x-2t)^2u=(x−2t)2. At t=0t=0t=0 this gives x2x^2x2, and differentiating gives ut=−4(x−2t)u_t=-4(x-2t)ut​=−4(x−2t) and 2ux=4(x−2t)2u_x=4(x-2t)2ux​=4(x−2t). The plus sign traces in the wrong direction, the shift by ttt uses speed one, and x2−2tx^2-2tx2−2t changes a value instead of moving its argument.

2. On the line, let ut+ux+u=xu_t+u_x+u=xut​+ux​+u=x and u(x,0)=0u(x,0)=0u(x,0)=0, with dimensionless variables. Find u(1,1)u(1,1)u(1,1) and round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Find the spatial position on the backward characteristic at time τ\tauτ before evaluating the source there.

The characteristic reaching (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) has position at time τ\tauτ given by x=τx=\taux=τ. Hence the source along it is τ\tauτ. The zero initial value contributes nothing. Duhamel’s formula gives u(1,1)=∫01e−(1−τ)τ ⁣dτ=e−1u(1,1)=\int_0^1\ee^{-(1-\tau)}\tau\dd\tau=\ee^{-1}u(1,1)=∫01​e−(1−τ)τdτ=e−1, using the primitive of τeτ\tau\ee^\tauτeτ, which is (τ−1)eτ(\tau-1)\ee^\tau(τ−1)eτ. The rounded value is 0.37. Evaluating the source at the final position throughout would use the wrong points.

3. Consider a one-dimensional flow with spatially varying speed a(x,t)a(x,t)a(x,t). The flow stretches every moving parcel. There are no sources. Which claim distinguishes a tracer value from the density of a conserved amount?

Hint. Use an interval whose two endpoints move with the flow. Its length can change.

For a tracer the material value stays constant, as expressed by ut+aux=0u_t+au_x=0ut​+aux​=0. For a density the amount in a moving interval stays constant. Expanding the flux derivative in ut+(au)x=0u_t+(au)_x=0ut​+(au)x​=0 gives ut+aux=−axuu_t+au_x=-a_xuut​+aux​=−ax​u. Thus density can fall as a parcel stretches. Assigning both quantities the tracer law or both the density law misses the distinction. Exchanging the laws puts the stretching term on the wrong quantity.

4. For ux+uy=0u_x+u_y=0ux​+uy​=0, prescribe u(ξ,ξ)=1u(\xi,\xi)=1u(ξ,ξ)=1 on an open segment of the line y=xy=xy=x. What happens to local existence and uniqueness near an interior point of that segment?

Hint. Compare the tangent of the data line to the characteristic direction and ask what the data determine on neighbouring characteristics.

The data line is itself a characteristic, with direction (1,1)(1,1)(1,1). The PDE requires the value to be constant along it, which the data satisfy. Any continuously differentiable FFF with F(0)=1F(0)=1F(0)=1 gives a solution u=F(y−x)u=F(y-x)u=F(y−x), so the solution need not be constant off the line and is not unique. Nonconstant values prescribed along this line would prevent existence. The noncharacteristic uniqueness argument requires a transverse tangent.
